name: Bilal Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies or government. We keep your answers confidential. What does a normal shift look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive haul trucks from the lower pit to the crusher, with a walk-round before the first load. I like the rhythm when dispatch keeps the queue moving. Each night I use an AI helper to sort my notes, but I still check the brakes and tyres myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew the new report helper is useful, but it doesn't know the feel of a loaded truck on wet gravel. I've been using AI to sort my own notes every evening and checking every line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm pleased if the ordinary job carries on. Our mortgage is covered and we have a good reserve, though I don't want a lazy report to hide a brake problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the haul truck and use the report helper for a month, then compare its entries with my paper log. I'd keep the savings transfer we already make after payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A tool that saves ten minutes is welcome if I still own the check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the helper miss last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The helper called a brake vibration normal because the numbers were within range. I wrote the mechanic a note anyway, and the pin was loose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend money on a new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the mine already provides the tablet. My partner Leena and I would leave the household budget as it is.

say: I'd tell my crew the **report helper** saves time when an operator checks each line against the machine.
I'd say **wet gravel** still needs a driver's judgment, whatever a tidy tablet report says.
think: I welcome the saved **minutes**, since our mortgage is covered and our reserve is strong.
I worry a missed **brake fault** could hide behind a report that looks perfectly neat.
do: Compare **tablet entries** with my paper fault log for one month while keeping the same truck shifts.
Continue the **payday transfer** into our household savings account at the current amount.
feel: **Calm** about income, with a watchful eye on machine safety.
S0.quote: The helper called a brake vibration normal because the numbers were within range.
fieldNote: His daily **AI use** is practical: he checks a report against a paper log and names a real loose pin.
His **reserve** and steady higher pay allow an unchanged budget; he still treats mechanical safety as his own responsibility.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck and compare tablet entries with the paper log
Continue the existing payday transfer into household savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell dispatch that if software can plan a cleaner queue, we should try it. I'd also tell the drivers that slower robot rollout means the cab work won't vanish overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatch roster might shrink while mine operators keep working. I'm curious about the new control screens, but I don't know whether the company would share better productivity with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to test the queue screen on one shift this month. In the first year I'd teach myself its alerts with the mine's training material and ask dispatch to log mistakes alongside the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for dispatch friends, but my own pay looks fairly safe while robots spread slowly. I can still imagine a better shift if queues improve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mistake would you report first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A queue screen that sends three trucks to the narrow mine turn at once would worry me. The safety officer knows that corner is a pinch point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would check the log with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with my friend Omar in dispatch at Friday handover. He sees the delays I can't see from the cab.

say: I'd say the **queue screen** deserves a trial if it cuts waiting without crowding the east turn.
I'd remind drivers the **robot** change comes more slowly than software for dispatch work.
think: I expect **dispatch** hours could shrink first, even while my own driving roster holds.
I'm unsure whether better **productivity** would turn into fairer pay for the people left on shift.
do: Volunteer for a **one-shift trial** of the queue screen and record errors at the east turn.
Learn its **alerts** from mine training material in the first year, then review delays with dispatch at handover.
feel: **Uneasy** for dispatch friends, while still interested in a smoother and safer shift.
S1.quote: A queue screen that sends three trucks to the narrow mine turn at once would worry me.
fieldNote: He volunteers early and focuses on a **specific hazard**, consistent with daily AI use and comfort with calculated risks.
He sees immediate **desk-work exposure** in dispatch but expects his cab pay to hold while robots spread slowly.

steps.text: Volunteer for a queue screen trial and log east-turn errors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2028 could rewrite our plans and reports, while 2031 is when hands-on machines may really challenge drivers. I want the dates on a board where everyone can see them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our savings could carry us for a while, but the mortgage and two children make a sudden cut in shifts serious. I'd be willing to move inside the mine if a real role exists; I don't assume one will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the control room lead for a trial shift now and map which equipment alerts a person must still check. After 2028 I'd apply for a remote operations course if the mine offers paid places, and keep six months of expenses untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I have a plan. The short gap to 2031 means I cannot treat a trial as a guarantee of a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leena at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Leena that six months of savings is a runway, not a landing place. We'd delay the kitchen renovation until we knew the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course isn't funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call the two nearby mines that already have control rooms and ask what entry skills they require. I would not pay for an unrecognised course.

say: I'd mark **2028** for planning and reports, then **2031** for possible hands-on machine competition.
I'd ask for visible **equipment dates** so drivers can judge whether there is time to train.
think: Our **savings** cover a spell without wages, but a sustained cut would still threaten the mortgage budget.
I'd consider a **control room** role if one exists, without assuming every driver can get one.
do: Ask for a **trial shift** in the control room now and list alerts that require a human check.
Apply for a **paid course** after 2028 if offered, while preserving six months of household expenses.
feel: **Anxious** about the short runway to robot competition, despite having savings and a possible route.
S2.quote: I'd tell my partner Leena that six months of savings is a runway, not a landing place.
fieldNote: He treats **2028** as a paperwork shift and **2031** as the possible driver-replacement point.
His proposed **course** requires paid places; the kitchen renovation is delayed until the roster becomes clearer.

steps.text: Ask control room lead for a trial shift and map equipment alerts
Apply for paid remote operations course if offered after 2028
Delay the kitchen renovation until the operator roster becomes clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew we have a few years to learn what the control room really does before 2034 brings possible robot drivers. The 2031 thinking change may make dispatch leaner much sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use five years to build a record of handling alerts, not just a certificate. Still, a company can cut a roster before the final machine arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for one control-room shift a month starting this year. I'd document the decisions I catch, then apply for the mine's internal control-room opening if one comes up after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned but steady. I can try a job before betting the family budget on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as proof you can do the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a log of real faults I caught and how I handed them to maintenance. A course completion alone doesn't show what happens at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a lower wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after we compared it with our mortgage payments and school costs. I might accept less for stable hours, but I wouldn't promise that today.

say: I'd tell drivers there is time to **test** control-room work before possible robot driving around 2034.
I'd point out **dispatch** may change in 2031 even while people remain in truck cabs.
think: I need a **fault record** that proves I can handle alerts, because a certificate alone might not secure a position.
A company might reduce **shifts** before robots arrive, so our savings cannot replace watching the roster.
do: Ask for **monthly control-room shifts** starting this year and record faults caught and handed to maintenance.
Apply for an **internal opening** after 2031 if the control room adds a position.
feel: **Uneasy** about the roster, with enough time and savings to test a new role carefully.
S3.quote: A course completion alone doesn't show what happens at three in the morning.
fieldNote: He seeks **practice** and a record of faults rather than treating a credential as a guaranteed transfer.
His wage choice remains **conditional** on comparing mortgage and school costs; he does not promise to accept less.

steps.text: Request one control-room shift each month and log faults caught
Apply for internal control-room opening if one appears after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to watch machines prove themselves and make a career decision. Reports may change by 2036, but hands-on robot work waits until about 2039 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then our children will be older and the mortgage may be smaller, though I won't count on that without making payments. I'd rather move toward training operators than wait for a final notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training manager this year what a mentor role requires and take one trainee on my next suitable shift. I'd keep our normal savings transfer, and after 2036 I'd apply for a formal trainer opening if the mine still has one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough to plan. Ten years lets me build experience before the machine question lands on the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new operator first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach the trainee to stop at the east turn when visibility drops, even if the screen says the queue is clear. A clean display never overrides a blind corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no trainer post exists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check nearby mines for safety and training roles before changing our family budget. I wouldn't leave a well-paid roster for a title on paper.

say: I'd say a **decade** gives operators time to test equipment and choose a path before possible robot driving around 2039.
I'd distinguish **2036** report changes from the later hands-on change in the cab.
think: Our **mortgage** may be smaller by then if we keep paying it, but I won't count future savings twice.
I'd rather build **training experience** than wait for a decision made entirely in an office.
do: Ask the **training manager** what a mentor role requires and take one trainee on a suitable shift.
Keep the normal **savings transfer**, then apply for a trainer opening after 2036 only if one exists.
feel: **Calm** enough to plan because time, savings and nearby mines leave room for choices.
S4.quote: A clean display never overrides a blind corner.
fieldNote: He shifts from a control-room experiment toward **mentoring** when the horizon stretches to a decade.
The trainer application is **conditional** on a real vacancy; he keeps his paid roster until the alternative is concrete.

steps.text: Ask training manager about mentoring and take one trainee on shift
Continue the normal household savings transfer
Apply for a trainer opening after 2036 if one exists

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most: 2028 could change the planning desk, and 2031 is close for anyone driving a truck. Paid control-room training and a clear equipment schedule would help me test a move before our savings carry the mortgage alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the machines when an alert looks ordinary but the driver feels something wrong. Drivers need a way to report missed equipment faults without being waved away by a clean screen.

headlineQuote: Drivers need a way to report missed equipment faults without being waved away by a clean screen.
portrait: **Bilal**, 43, drives haul trucks at a large mine; his vocational certificate and higher pay support a partner, children and mortgage.
He uses **AI daily** to sort notes, checks every result and volunteers early when a new queue screen can be tested safely.
His strong **savings** and nearby mines create options, but the 2028-to-2031 gap makes lost shifts a real household concern.
With more **time**, he seeks fault-handling experience, tests control-room work and considers mentoring before any trainer vacancy becomes real.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only about three years before hands-on robots may threaten the truck driving that funds his household.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **control-room training** and a clear equipment schedule would let him test another role while savings still cover the mortgage.
